summary: Meyer's reply to RFC 467, describing the lost allocation and half-closed connection problems of the Host-Host protocol and offering comments and alternative suggestions on the BBN proposal. It reviews how connections and allocation worked at the time. It updates RFC 467.

plainLanguage.summary: Someone commented on a plan to fix stuck network conversations, explained the trouble, and suggested other ways to solve it.

questions: what is the lost allocate problem
subtitle: A 1973 reply to a proposed fix for stuck ARPANET connections, arguing the real problem is lost messages.

tldr.problem: RFC 467 proposed fixes for two annoying failures of the Host-Host protocol: connections that stall after a lost allocation message, and connections left half-closed after a host crash.
tldr.mechanism: E. Meyer of MIT-Multics opposes both fixes. He suggests a modified Give-Back (GVB) and Return Allocation (RET) exchange that detects lost messages, plus five principles for stricter use of Reset Host (RST) and error reporting.
tldr.outcome: This is a comment document, not a specification. It argues that hiding lost messages is dangerous and that errors should be made visible instead.

sections.title: The Two Problems from RFC 467
sections.content:
This memo answers RFC 467, from Burchfiel and Tomlinson of BBN. Under the Host-Host protocol, a connection starts when one host sends a Request for Connection and the other replies. The host at the read end then controls data flow with allocation control messages. The writing host may send only as much data as the allocation permits, and must wait for a new allocation when it runs out.

The first problem is the lost allocate phenomenon. If an allocate message is lost, the sender waits for more allocation while the reader believes it already gave it and waits for data. A lost data message has similar symptoms. The connection is blocked permanently, and the only cure at the time was to disconnect and reconnect.

The second is the half-closed phenomenon. One host crashes and purges its tables, while the other still believes the connection is open and refuses a new request for the same socket.
sections.plainLanguage: Two kids pass notes saying how many more notes they may send. If one note is lost, both wait forever. Or one kid forgets the game and the other still thinks it is on.

sections.title: What RFC 467 Proposed and Why Meyer Objects
sections.content:
For lost allocates, RFC 467 adds a pair of messages, Reset Connection by Sender (RCS) and Reset Connection by Receiver (RCR). Either side may zero its allocation counter and send one; the other zeros its own and replies, so both sides agree again. For half-closed connections, a host that finds an inconsistency silently closes its end, either on receiving an Error Report or on a connection request for sockets it thinks are still connected.

Meyer's group at Project MAC opposes both, strongly for the resynchronization. His view is that this is really a lost message problem. Resetting counters papers over the symptom, and a data message lost in the middle of a file could have disastrous, undetected consequences. He sees the true fixes as removing the cause of undetected loss or moving to a protocol designed for an unreliable path.

On half-closed connections he objects that assuming the state of the foreign NCP can mask bugs, and that the proposal misses cases such as another socket trying to connect to the dead connection's socket.
sections.plainLanguage: The first plan is to reset everything when stuck. The reply says that hides the real trouble, which is that messages are going missing, and that could break important things quietly.

sections.title: Meyer's Alternatives
sections.content:
As an interim fix for allocation, Meyer modifies the existing commands. A receiving host may at any time send a Give-Back allocation (GVB) message with both fraction fields set to all 1s, which keeps compatibility with the current protocol, where it means return everything. The sender stops, waits for the RFNM of its last message (an empty pipeline), then sends RET returning all remaining allocation.

The reader then compares the returned allocation with its own counters. If they match, no message was lost and it sends a new allocation. If not, handling is a local option, but at minimum a host should report the error to the user and to a person responsible for network performance.

For half-closed connections he favors more rigorous use of the existing Reset Host (RST) message, and lists five principles. An NCP should purge connections to a host reported dead (Imp-to-Host type 7), answer other traffic from it with RST, and exchange RST and RRP before first communicating. It should abort a connection with CLS if an Incomplete Transmission (type 9) cannot be retransmitted. And on an inconsistent message it should send ERR and discard it, rather than change its own state.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of a blind reset, the reader asks the writer to hand back all its permission and checks the numbers match. If they do not, someone notices that a note was lost.

sections.title: Why It Matters
sections.content:
The memo is a snapshot of an early argument about whether a protocol should quietly recover from errors or expose them. Meyer prefers the second: the GVB/RET scheme gives positive indication that an error occurred, while RCS/RCR conceals errors. He admits it cannot start a check from either side, but calls that a minor disadvantage.

The document ends with a note that it was put into machine readable form for the online RFC archives by Helene Morin in December 1999.
sections.plainLanguage: The big idea is that it is better to notice and report a problem than to quietly cover it up.

references.text: Burchfiel, J. and R. Tomlinson, Network Request for Comments 467, BBN.
